p: Tiago taped HEARTH's floor plan onto the high bay concrete, with a red X for the hatch at one end.
Helen walked it and told them about a galley fire on the old station nine years ago, when the last crew member out had earplugs in and his door shut.
The team wrote each emergency from all four bunks, and quarter four, the far quarter half behind the hygiene wall, became everyone's worry.
Then Jun timed a depressurization run with Halo's crew trainers, and the hatch didn't close until a hundred and thirty three seconds.
The scenario allows a hundred and twenty, and quarter four is the last one out.
Jun Takeda. Junior engineer. He keeps the model and timed the walk.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He stood in quarter four and saw the problem.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He taped HEARTH out on the floor.
Odette. Safety engineer. She wants every scenario in seconds.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She still carries her fire note.
Amara Osei. Program manager, holding the schedule to the requirements review.
New in this chapter: Beto Salinas.
Somebody had written 133 on the whiteboard in the HEARTH room in red marker, and nobody erased it. By Monday of week five Wes had drawn a box around it. Nobody asked him why.

The number sat over everyone's head while Jun printed the first draft of the system requirements. It came to four hundred lines and nineteen pages, and he carried it to Nadia's desk with both hands like something that might spill.
It's everything, he said. Every stakeholder requirement, turned into what the module has to do. I didn't sleep much.

Nadia started reading at her desk and finished in the high bay, sitting on an equipment case at the edge of the blue tape, with a red pen she hadn't meant to uncap. Some of it was very good. Line forty one said the cabin shall be quiet. Line ninety tried to do the whole hatch in one sentence. Line two hundred and six said the module shall be safe.
She could hear Colleen already. You can't fly a line that says be safe.

The system requirements review was at the end of week six. After that, these four hundred lines would be the baseline, the thing every drawing, every test and every argument for the next two and a half years would point back to. She uncapped the pen the rest of the way.
Tuesday Nadia sat down with Jun and the red-marked draft. He looked at the ink and then at her.
Most of the lines traced to a scenario on the tape. Some of the language, though, would never survive a test engineer.

They take ten lines together, slowly: is it necessary, is there one reading, can it be checked, is it one thing, can it be built, where did it come from. By the twentieth line Jun is finding the problems before she does.
Line ninety was the hatch. "The hatch shall open within 10 seconds and seal to the leak limit and be operable by one crew member from either side."
It's all about the hatch, Jun said. Isn't it cleaner in one place?
Three lines, three parents, three verification methods: test for the opening time, test for the leak rate, demonstration for one person operation. Jun renumbers them and looks pleased about it.
Wes wanted the requirements in a spreadsheet, the way FRO had always kept them, one tab per subsystem. Jun wanted them in the model, linked to the stakeholder needs and the scenarios.
I can read a spreadsheet, Wes said. Everybody can read a spreadsheet.

Jun runs the first trace report that afternoon. Twelve requirements have no parent. Four needs have no requirement under them at all. Wes reads the spreadsheet view and says it looks like a spreadsheet, which is as close to approval as he gets.

Line forty one, the cabin shall be quiet, came from a stakeholder requirement about crew sleep. Helen's notes said the old station was so loud that some crews slept with earplugs every night, and under that, underlined: if it's quiet, they don't need earplugs, and they hear the alarm.
Tiago read it over Nadia's shoulder. How do I test quiet?
They set 45 dBA at the head of each sleep station, with the module in its sleep mode, and trace it to crew sleep. Tiago nods. That I can put a microphone on.
Odette came to Wednesday's requirements meeting with a hazard list and one page of proposed safety requirements. The first hazard was the hatch opening by accident while the module was pressurized.
That one's catastrophic, she said. So. What has to break for that hatch to open with air behind it?
Jun links the requirement to the hazard and gives it a verification method. Odette reads the wording, changes one word, and initials it.
Helen's comments came back Thursday. On the egress requirement she'd crossed out the value and written 60 seconds, and under it, smaller: that's as long as I can watch the clock.
Jun pulled up the tape times. It took forty five seconds just to wake up and get out of a bunk.

Helen looks at the wake times for a long minute. I know, she says. I wanted to see it in writing that I can't have it. They settle on the time Halo's reference leak allows, with the rationale written under it. The current layout doesn't meet it, but some layout can, and that's the design's problem to solve.

Saturday she met Beto Salinas for coffee in Castle Rock, which Beto called halfway and wasn't. He'd been her bench partner at the avionics shop in Colorado Springs, and he was still there. He took her laptop without asking, scrolled to the verification column, and laughed out loud.

Test. Test. Test. Test, he read. You still love a green PASS, Brooks. He knew why. He'd never once asked her about it, which was one of the reasons they were still friends. Same job, different hardware, he said, and pushed the laptop back across the table. So do it the way you used to.

They do sixty lines over two refills. Labels go to inspection, the hatch handle to demonstration, leak rate to test, and fifteen years of debris to analysis. Beto steals the last of her muffin as his fee.
One requirement made Tiago put his coffee down. The shielding had to keep the probability of a penetrating micrometeoroid or debris strike below a set value over fifteen years in orbit.
Then he picked it back up and grinned. There's a light gas gun in Ohio. It shoots panels, not years. The question was what to call the rest of the proof.
Tiago books the gas gun for a dozen sample panels. The shots calibrate the model, and the model covers fifteen years. I can stand behind that, he says.

Halo's program office called Monday of week six. They wanted edit access to FRO's requirements in the model before the review, so their engineers could fix wording directly instead of sending comments.
It would save a week of email, Amara said. Your call.

Halo sees the current set every day and comments on the line itself. FRO's people make the edits, and every one has a name and a reason. Halo's lead engineer says it's better than what they asked for.

The set froze for review on Tuesday of week six. On Wednesday Wes dropped a sticky note on Nadia's keyboard with three lines in his square capitals. Hatch handle on both sides, one hand, no tools. Seat track down both sides of the aisle for stowage. All harnesses in the overhead channel.
Obvious stuff, he said. Every cargo module had them. Just put them in.
Wes looks at the three forms and then at her. Paperwork. He fills in the rationale anyway, two lines each, and they're good lines. The requests go into the queue with numbers.
Amara set up the first configuration control board for Friday after the review. Wes's three change requests were the first items on it. She asked Nadia what the board would need to decide.
Wes, passing, said the board would need about thirty seconds.

Jun runs the trace. The hatch handle maps cleanly to a need. The seat track narrows the aisle by eleven centimeters, and the egress model gets slower. The overhead harness touches two interfaces nobody has defined yet. The board has something real to decide.
The night before the review Jun's trace report came to three hundred and ninety six requirements. Eleven still had values marked to be determined, including the egress layout's test conditions.
Wes wanted the review pushed until the open values were closed. Amara wanted to baseline it and stop talking about it.
The review package lists all eleven on one page: who, by when, and from what analysis. The reviewers ask about three of them, and all three have answers.
The night before the review Nadia was still at her desk at nine when her phone lit up.
A text from Dad. BIG DAY TOMORROW. ROSIE DREW YOU A NEW ROCKET. 5 IN THE WINDOW NOW. SHE PUT YOU IN. CALLIE SAYS YOU MISSED SUNDAY. SHE WONT SAY IT SO IM SAYING IT.

She read it at her desk with the review package open on the other screen. She typed an apology and deleted it. What she sent was shorter: she'd call Callie Sunday, and Rosie should save her the window seat. Then she put Sunday at noon in her calendar with an alarm on it, and sat there a minute with nothing to check.

The review ran all of Thursday in the big conference room. Helen was on the screen from Halo, and an observer from OCSC sat in the back writing in a notebook nobody got to see. Jun presented the trace. Tiago presented the verification methods. Odette walked through the hazard controls without once raising her voice.

At four the chair read the result: proceed, with four action items. The requirements baseline was set. Helen said, on the screen, that it was the first requirements set she'd read that sounded like it had met a crew. Amara shook Nadia's hand in the hallway and didn't say anything about the schedule, which was new.
Wes's three change requests sat in the board's queue for Friday, numbered, with his rationale in his square capitals. Outside the baseline, where they belonged until somebody decided.
Friday morning Nadia went to the structures area to borrow the latest hatch drawing. It was on Wes's plotter, still warm, revision C. She read the notes block out of habit.

HEARTH primary structure, hatch and aisle, rev C, notes block (excerpt). 7. HATCH HANDLE BOTH SIDES. ONE HAND. NO TOOLS.. 8. SEAT TRACK BOTH SIDES OF AISLE, FULL LENGTH.. 9. ALL HARNESS ROUTED IN OVERHEAD CHANNEL.. Drawn: W. Harland. Date: Wk 6 Mon.
Three notes, drawn into the structure three days before anybody had decided them. The aisle on the drawing was already eleven centimeters narrower than the aisle on the tape.
The baseline was fourteen hours old. Wes's drawing was three days older.
The board met at ten to decide whether Wes could have what he'd already drawn. Nadia rolled the sheet under her arm and walked it over to him first.
